issues.legal_issue: A non-retrospective statutory amendment removing a pre-emption right does not defeat a decree already granted in a pending appeal.
material_facts: A co-sharer brought a pre-emption suit under the then-applicable law, and the trial court decreed the suit.
The claimant deposited the purchase money as required after the decree, and the decree was affirmed on appeal.
While a further appeal was pending, an amendment substituted the provision governing pre-emption and limited the right to tenants; the amendment did not state that it applied retrospectively.
issues.conclusion: The amendment did not affect the parties’ substantive rights fixed by the trial court decree. The appellate court was not required to apply the substituted provision, and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A substantive right is governed by the law in force when the suit is commenced or adjudicated unless the later enactment applies retrospectively expressly or by necessary intendment. An appeal may be a continuation of the suit, but that does not authorize applying a prospective enactment to impair an accrued or vested right. Order 20 Rule 14 CPC provides for transfer of title upon the pre-emption decree-holder’s deposit of the purchase money. The Court approved Didar Singh v. Ishar Singh and Shantidevi v. Hukum Chand, and held that Ramjilal v. Ghisa Ram did not state the correct law; it distinguished the retrospective enactments considered in Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, Ram Sarup v. Munshi and Amir Singh v. Ram Singh.

rule.if: preemption_suit_appeal and first_instance_decree_for_claimant and purchase_money_deposited and amendment_has_no_retroactive_intent

predicates.preemption_suit_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a suit seeking pre-emption of a sale.
predicates.first_instance_decree_for_claimant: The court of first instance granted the claimant a decree for pre-emption.
predicates.purchase_money_deposited: The claimant deposited the purchase money after the decree.
predicates.amendment_has_no_retroactive_intent: The later amendment contains no express or necessarily implied intention to apply retrospectively.

issues.definition: When a claimant has obtained a pre-emption decree and deposited the purchase money, an appeal in that suit does not allow a non-retrospective amendment to defeat the decree.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-emption claimant’s post-decree loss of qualification does not defeat a decree where the claimant possessed the right at the legally relevant stages and the right became vested.
material_facts: The claimant asserted a co-sharer’s pre-emption right arising from a sale.
The trial court granted the pre-emption decree, and the claimant deposited the purchase money.
The claimant’s asserted loss of qualification arose after the trial court decree, during the appeal; the subsequent statutory change was not retrospective.
issues.conclusion: The claimant had to establish the pre-emption right on the date of sale, the date of suit and the date of the trial court decree. A subsequent loss of qualification or change in law that is not retrospective did not defeat the decree on appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under the pre-emption authorities, including Hans Nath v. Ragho Prasad Singh, Bhagwan Das v. Chet Ram, Rikhi Ram v. Ram Kumar and Didar Singh v. Ishar Singh, qualification must subsist through the trial court’s decree, but a later loss ordinarily does not affect the claim. Under Order 20 Rule 14 CPC, after the decree-holder deposits the purchase money, title vests in the claimant. The appellate court reviews the correctness of the trial court’s decision on the rights existing at the time of adjudication; later events cannot be used to impair that vested right unless a retrospective law requires it.

rule.if: preemption_suit_appeal and claimant_qualified_at_relevant_stages and first_instance_decree_for_claimant and purchase_money_deposited and later_change_is_nonretroactive

predicates.preemption_suit_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a suit seeking pre-emption of a sale.
predicates.claimant_qualified_at_relevant_stages: The claimant possessed the pre-emption qualification on the sale date, the suit date and the date of the trial court decree.
predicates.first_instance_decree_for_claimant: The court of first instance granted the claimant a decree for pre-emption.
predicates.purchase_money_deposited: The claimant deposited the purchase money after the decree.
predicates.later_change_is_nonretroactive: The claimant’s loss of qualification or the change in law occurred after the decree and does not apply retrospectively.

issues.definition: If a qualified claimant obtains a pre-emption decree and deposits the purchase money, a later non-retrospective change does not undo the decree.

issues.legal_issue: A clear amendment affecting substantive rights is not retrospective merely because it substitutes a provision or is beneficial, and it is not declaratory without an intention to clarify or explain the prior law.
material_facts: The amendment substituted a plain and unambiguous provision limiting the right of pre-emption to tenants.
The prior provision was also clear, and the amendment did not expressly or by necessary implication address pending claims or declare what the prior law meant.
The amendment affected the substantive pre-emption rights at issue.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was prospective, was not declaratory, and could not be made retrospective through benevolent construction.
issues.legal_principle: A statute affecting substantive rights is presumed prospective unless retrospective operation is expressed or necessarily implied; procedural changes are generally presumed retrospective, subject to limits. A declaratory or explanatory enactment clarifies the prior law or supplies an obvious omission, and its substance—not merely its label—determines its character. Benevolent construction cannot add words to a clear provision or re-legislate it. The Court relied on Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry, Dayawati v. Inderjit, Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra, K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala, Moti Ram v. Suraj Bhan, Keshavlal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas and R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan; it distinguished Rafiquennessa v. Lal Bahadur Chetri and H. Shiva Rao v. Celelia Pereira, whose statutory contexts or ambiguity differed.

rule.if: substantive_right_affected and amendment_text_clear and no_retroactive_intent and no_prior_law_clarification and preemption_case_pending_on_appeal

predicates.substantive_right_affected: The amendment changes a substantive right rather than merely regulating procedure.
predicates.amendment_text_clear: The amendment’s language is plain and unambiguous.
predicates.no_retroactive_intent: The amendment contains no express or necessarily implied intention to operate retrospectively.
predicates.no_prior_law_clarification: The amendment does not clarify an ambiguity or supply an omission in the prior law.
predicates.preemption_case_pending_on_appeal: A pre-emption claim is pending in an appeal when the amendment takes effect.

issues.definition: In a pending pre-emption appeal, a clear amendment changing substantive rights operates prospectively when it neither indicates retrospective intent nor clarifies prior law.
